..
As of 300 PM Wednesday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... Staying above average through tomorrow. A cold 
front Thursday brings much cooler weather by early Friday.

The above average temperature, albeit short-lived prior to a cold 
front tomorrow evening, will continue today and most of the day 
tomorrow. Widespread low to middle 70s are expected this afternoon, 
followed by upper 60s to lower 70s on Thursday, about 8-12 degrees 
above seasonal normals.

Satellite imagery currently shows a weak disturbance at mid-levels 
tracking east across the Deep South this afternoon and evening. It 
will increase our clouds through the day/evening, but we stay dry.

Low pressure across the Mid MS Valley today will reach the Mid-
Atlantic states Thursday, before exiting off the New England coast 
early Friday. A pre-frontal trough will be in place tomorrow ahead 
of a cold front forecast to move through during the evening hours. A 
persistent west-southwest flow Thursday should keep us still mild 
most of the day, with the colder air not arriving until overnight. 
Low-level thicknesses take a nose dive to around 1320-1325m by 
Friday morning, typical of early December. But with a well mixed 
boundary layer, forecast lows should range in the upper 30s NW to 
low 40s SE.

Ahead of the front, a pair of shortwaves rotating around the larger 
trough will provide enough height falls to warrant a widely isolated 
shower or sprinkle in the morning across the Triad and eastern areas 
in the late afternoon to early evening. Most areas are forecast to 
remain dry with little moisture below cloud layer. Wind gusts 
along/ahead of the front will gust to 25-30 mph, highest across the 
northwest. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... Behind a secondary cold front on Friday, the 
chilliest air of the season will arrive and support the first 
widespread frost/freeze risk this weekend. This will be followed by 
continued below average temperatures and dry conditions that will 
persist through most of next week.

Broad mid/upper troughing over the Eastern US on Friday will 
gradually weaken and shift into the North Atlantic through the 
weekend. At the surface, low pressure centered just east of southern 
New England early Friday will slowly lift NE. This will have dragged 
a cold front through central NC on Thursday, and a reinforcing cold 
front is expected to cross the area on Friday. This secondary cold 
front will be accompanied by another vorticity lobe and associated 
mid-level height falls rotating around the base of the broader 
trough on Friday late afternoon and evening. Model soundings 
indicate potential for a thin layer of very weak instability and 
saturation centered around 800 mb during this time, which may be 
enough to squeeze out some isolated sprinkles or light rain, if 
precipitation can reach the ground despite a fairly dry sub-cloud 
layer and PW values only 50-70% of normal. The 12z ECMWF/GFS/CMC 
ensembles had an uptick in probabilities of measurable 
precipitation, but their mean QPF is still around 0.05" or less. The 
best chance still appears to be across the NE Piedmont and 
northern/central Coastal Plain. 

Temperatures will turn below normal on Friday in a CAA regime, with 
highs in the mid 50s to lower 60s. We look to stay fairly mixed on 
Friday night, which will limit radiational cooling, but forecast 
lows are still in the 30s, resulting in some frost/freeze concerns. 
Wind chills could also drop to the mid 20s to lower 30s. As Canadian 
high pressure builds into the Eastern US, the MSLP gradient will 
relax, resulting in calmer conditions on Sunday and especially 
Monday mornings. This is when the first sub-freezing temperatures of 
the season are expected across much of central NC, with a hard 
freeze even possible over outlying parts of the Piedmont. Thus the 
growing season is likely to be ended this weekend. For reference, 
the last day GSO reached at or below freezing was March 18, while it 
was April 9 at RDU and March 29 at FAY. Highs on Saturday and Sunday 
will also be chilly, only reaching the lower to mid 50s both days. 
These would be the coldest highs across the area since March. 

Fire weather concerns can't be totally ruled out on Friday and 
Saturday given RH values dropping to 30-40% and possibly even lower 
given NW downsloping flow. However, momentum transfer on forecast 
model soundings indicates marginal wind gusts both days (in the 15-
20 kt range). This combined with the cool temperatures will limit 
potential for increased fire danger.

The Canadian High will remain over the Eastern US from Monday 
through Wednesday, with only slow weakening/modification expected. 
So temperatures will remain below normal through the period.
